items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The ability to understand that other people have thoughts, beliefs and feelings that may differ from one’s own”?
items.answer: Theory of mind
items.markingKey: Theory of mind: the ability to understand that other people have thoughts, beliefs and feelings that may differ from one’s own. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Adults with Asperger syndrome may pass simple theory of mind tests. Reason (R): Simple tests designed for children are too easy for intelligent adults. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Ceiling effects explain why a more advanced adult test was needed. [1]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by theory of mind and why it is important.
items.answer: Theory of mind is understanding that others have their own beliefs, intentions and emotions; it allows us to predict and interpret behaviour and to communicate effectively.
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark importance [2]

items.stem: Tomás, an adult in Toronto, says that conversations at work are confusing because colleagues often mean something different from what they say. Use the concept of theory of mind to explain Tomás’s difficulty.
items.answer: Tomás may find it harder to infer other people’s intentions and feelings from cues such as the eyes and tone, so implied meanings are missed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark theory of mind; 1 mark application [2]

items.stem: Isla, an adult in Mexico City, says that conversations at work are confusing because colleagues often mean something different from what they say. (a) Suggest how Isla’s theory of mind could be measured. (b) Explain one reason why a low score would not prove that Isla is autistic.
items.answer: (a) Using the Revised Eyes Test: choosing which of four words best describes what a person in a photo of the eyes is thinking or feeling (36 items). (b) The Eyes Test is not a diagnostic tool; scores also depend on vocabulary, attention and cultural familiarity with the faces.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark test; 1 mark description [2] (b) 1 mark not diagnostic; 1 mark other factors [2]

items.stem: Explain why Baron-Cohen et al. needed a more sensitive “advanced” test of theory of mind.
items.answer: Adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism often pass simple false-belief tasks, yet still have social difficulties, so a harder test was needed to detect subtle differences.

items.stem: “Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including ecological validity in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (validity of the Eyes Test): The revision added more items and four choices, reducing ceiling effects and chance guessing, and the AS/HFA group scored lowest as predicted, supporting the test’s validity. Strength (quantitative data): Eyes Test scores out of 36 allowed groups to be compared objectively (for example a mean of 21.9 for the AS/HFA group versus 28.0 for students). Weakness (generalisability): The AS/HFA group was small (15) and all male, so the findings may not apply to all autistic people, including women. Weakness (ecological validity): Judging emotions from still photographs of eyes is unlike everyday social interaction, where faces move and there are voices and context. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. items.stem: Evaluate Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ecological validity.
items.answer: Strength (individual versus situational explanations): The study shows individual differences in theory of mind (and by sex), supporting an individual explanation of social understanding. Strength (standardisation): Every participant saw the same 36 photographs with the same four word choices and had access to a glossary, so the test was standardised and comparable across groups. Weakness (generalisability): The AS/HFA group was small (15) and all male, so the findings may not apply to all autistic people, including women. Weakness (ecological validity): Judging emotions from still photographs of eyes is unlike everyday social interaction, where faces move and there are voices and context. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: A researcher in Toronto is interested in whether there is a relationship between empathy and the number of friends people have. Plan a correlation to test this. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, ethical issues, a hypothesis and how the data will be presented.
items.answer: Method: a correlation. Measure both co-variables for each participant (for example with a rating scale) and plot a scatter graph; look for direction and strength of the relationship. Variables: co-variable 1: empathy score; co-variable 2: number of close friends. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Toronto, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: What is meant by ‘theory of mind’?
items.answer: The ability to understand that other people have thoughts, beliefs and feelings that may differ from one’s own.
items.markingKey: Theory of mind: the ability to understand that other people have thoughts, beliefs and feelings that may differ from one’s own. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: In a revision session, a student says: “The IQ-matched group helped to show that low Eyes Test scores were not simply due to low intelligence.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Group 4 was matched on IQ with the AS/HFA group but scored much higher.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test in terms of ecological validity.
items.answer: Judging emotions from still photographs of eyes is unlike everyday social interaction, where faces move and there are voices and context.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ethan compared Eyes Test scores (out of 36) for 8 adults with an autism diagnosis and 8 adults without, matched for age and IQ, in Kathmandu. items.answer: Volunteer sampling. Weakness: volunteers may share characteristics (for example being more curious or helpful), so the sample is self-selected and may not represent the target population.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test. Include at least one point about validity of the Eyes Test.
items.answer: Strength (validity of the Eyes Test): The revision added more items and four choices, reducing ceiling effects and chance guessing, and the AS/HFA group scored lowest as predicted, supporting the test’s validity. Strength (standardisation): Every participant saw the same 36 photographs with the same four word choices and had access to a glossary, so the test was standardised and comparable across groups. Weakness (the student sample): Group 3 were Cambridge students, who are not typical of the general population in age or education. Weakness (generalisability): The AS/HFA group was small (15) and all male, so the findings may not apply to all autistic people, including women. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain what is meant by theory of mind and why it is important. (b) A student writes: “Theory of mind means being able to read other people’s minds accurately all the time.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Theory of mind is understanding that others have their own beliefs, intentions and emotions; it allows us to predict and interpret behaviour and to communicate effectively. (b) Not correct. It is the understanding that others have mental states, used to infer them; everyone makes mistakes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark definition; 1 mark importance [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: With reference to Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test, explain one strength relating to individual versus situational explanations.
items.answer: The study shows individual differences in theory of mind (and by sex), supporting an individual explanation of social understanding.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to individual versus situational explanations; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Zara, an adult in Bangkok, says that conversations at work are confusing because colleagues often mean something different from what they say. Suggest how Zara’s theory of mind could be measured.
items.answer: Using the Revised Eyes Test: choosing which of four words best describes what a person in a photo of the eyes is thinking or feeling (36 items).
items.markingKey: 1 mark test; 1 mark description [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the four groups of participants in Baron-Cohen et al.’s study. (b) A student writes: “In the Revised Eyes Test, participants saw photographs of whole faces.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Group 1: 15 adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism (all male). Group 2: 122 adults from the general population. Group 3: 103 Cambridge undergraduates. Group 4: 14 adults from the general population matched on IQ with Group 1. (b) Not correct. They saw only the eye region.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per group [4] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe the main results of Baron-Cohen et al.’s study.
items.answer: The AS/HFA group scored significantly lower on the Eyes Test (mean 21.9) than the other groups (26.2, 28.0, 30.9); they scored higher on the AQ; Eyes Test and AQ scores correlated negatively; females in the general population scored higher than males.
items.markingKey: 1 mark AS/HFA lowest; 1 mark correlation; 1 mark sex difference [3]

items.stem: “Baron-Cohen et al.’s (2001) study of the Revised Eyes Test has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including the student sample in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (standardisation): Every participant saw the same 36 photographs with the same four word choices and had access to a glossary, so the test was standardised and comparable across groups. Strength (individual versus situational explanations): The study shows individual differences in theory of mind (and by sex), supporting an individual explanation of social understanding. Weakness (generalisability): The AS/HFA group was small (15) and all male, so the findings may not apply to all autistic people, including women. Weakness (the student sample): Group 3 were Cambridge students, who are not typical of the general population in age or education. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Define the term ‘autism spectrum condition’.
items.answer: A developmental condition involving differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive interests.

items.stem: ‘The Revised Eyes Test is a valid measure of theory of mind.’ Discuss this view. In your answer, you may refer to standardisation and generalisability.
items.answer: Arguments for: Adults with AS/HFA scored significantly lower than all comparison groups, as predicted. Scores correlated negatively with the AQ. The revised version reduced ceiling effects and guessing. Arguments against: Recognising emotion in still photos of eyes is a narrow task, unlike real social interaction. Some words are complex, so vocabulary may affect scores despite the glossary. The photos were mostly of white faces, which may disadvantage other groups. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
